problems.title: Design an ATM Machine
problems.summary: Design an ATM with card authentication, balance enquiry, withdrawal and deposit, using the State pattern for the session flow and Chain of Responsibility for cash dispensing.
keyPoints: Session flow is a State machine: Idle -> CardInserted -> Authenticated -> Idle on eject or block.
Default methods in the state interface reject invalid actions; each state overrides only what it allows.
Cash dispensing uses Chain of Responsibility across note handlers (2000 -> 500 -> 200 -> 100).
Plan dispensing first, then debit the account, then commit notes, so money is never debited without cash.
BankService interface hides the bank; PIN attempts and card blocking live on the bank side.
Validate amounts (positive, multiple of 100, daily limit) before touching balances.
Discuss reversals for network failures and idempotent transaction ids.

interviewQuestions.q: Why use the State pattern in an ATM?
interviewQuestions.a: The valid operations depend entirely on the session phase: you cannot enter a PIN without a card or withdraw before authentication. With State, each phase is a class that implements only its allowed operations and triggers transitions, while the `ATM` context delegates. Default interface methods throw meaningful errors for invalid actions. New phases (admin mode, out-of-service) are new classes rather than new branches in every method.

interviewQuestions.q: How does Chain of Responsibility help in dispensing cash?
interviewQuestions.a: Each cassette is a handler for one note value. The request (amount) enters the 2000 handler, which uses as many notes as it can given its count and passes the remainder to the 500 handler, and so on. If the last handler still has a remainder, the amount cannot be dispensed. Adding or removing denominations means relinking handlers, not changing logic. I plan first without mutating counts and commit only after the account debit succeeds.

interviewQuestions.q: What if the bank debits the account but the ATM fails to dispense?
interviewQuestions.a: That is a distributed consistency problem. First, minimise it by verifying that the dispenser can produce the amount before debiting. Second, record each withdrawal with a unique transaction id and state (INITIATED, DEBITED, DISPENSED). If dispensing fails after the debit, the ATM sends a reversal (compensating credit) referencing the same id; the bank processes it idempotently. Reconciliation jobs compare ATM journals with bank records to catch anything left over.

interviewQuestions.q: Where should PIN validation and attempt counting happen?
interviewQuestions.a: On the bank side, not in the ATM. The ATM forwards the PIN (encrypted with hardware security modules in reality) and the bank validates it, increments failed attempts and blocks the card after three failures. This keeps the policy consistent across all ATMs and channels, so a user cannot reset the counter by moving to another machine. The ATM only reacts to the result: retry, proceed, or retain the card.

problems.title: Design a Chess Game
problems.summary: A lighter but complete chess design: board, polymorphic pieces with move rules, turn management, capture and check detection, with notes on castling and en passant.
keyPoints: Each piece subclass overrides canMove with its geometry; shared helpers handle straight and diagonal sliding.
The board validates path clearance for sliding pieces; knights skip the path check.
Game validation pipeline: piece exists, correct turn, not capturing own piece, geometry, no self-check.
Self-check is detected by simulating the move, testing if the king is attacked, then reverting.
Checkmate = in check with no legal moves; stalemate = not in check with no legal moves.
Moves are Command-like records in a history stack for undo, en passant and notation.
Scope clearly: castling, en passant and promotion are typical extensions, not P0.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you avoid a giant switch on piece type?
interviewQuestions.a: Make `Piece` abstract with an abstract `canMove(board, from, to)` and let each subclass implement its geometry - runtime polymorphism. Shared helpers in the base class (`straight`, `diagonal`) avoid duplication, so `Queen` is just `straight || diagonal`. The game calls `piece.canMove(...)` without knowing the type. Adding a fairy piece (say, an Archbishop combining bishop and knight) means one new class, satisfying the Open/Closed Principle.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you detect that a move leaves the king in check?
interviewQuestions.a: Temporarily apply the move on the board, find the mover's king, and check whether any opponent piece can move to that square (`isAttacked`), then restore the original pieces. If the king is attacked, the move is illegal. This handles pinned pieces and moving the king into check uniformly. For efficiency, engines compute attack maps incrementally, but simulate-and-revert is the clear and correct approach for an interview.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you implement castling?
interviewQuestions.a: Track whether the king and each rook have moved (a `hasMoved` flag updated on every move, restored on undo). Castling is legal when neither has moved, the squares between them are empty, the king is not currently in check, and the squares the king passes through and lands on are not attacked. The move relocates both king and rook, so it is best modelled as a special `Move` subtype (`CastleMove`) whose execute and undo handle both pieces.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you support undo in chess?
interviewQuestions.a: Store each executed move as an object containing from, to, the moving piece, the captured piece, and any special-state changes (castling rights, en passant square, promotion piece, hasMoved flags). Push it onto a history stack. Undo pops the last move and restores everything it recorded, then switches the turn back. This is the Command pattern; the same history also generates PGN notation and supports replay.

problems.title: Design a Hotel Booking System
problems.summary: Design a hotel reservation system with room types, date-range availability, overlap-safe booking, pricing strategies and cancellation.
keyPoints: Use half-open date ranges [checkIn, checkOut); ranges overlap iff s1 < e2 and s2 < e1.
Keep bookings per room in a TreeMap keyed by check-in for O(log n) overlap checks via lowerEntry.
Lock per room so bookings for different rooms proceed concurrently without double booking.
Pricing and cancellation refunds are Strategies; weekend surcharges computed per night.
Booking lifecycle transitions are guarded: CONFIRMED -> CHECKED_IN -> CHECKED_OUT or CANCELLED.
DateRange as an immutable record encapsulates validation and overlap logic.
At scale, OTAs track per-date inventory counts per room type and enforce uniqueness in the database.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you check if a room is available for a date range efficiently?
interviewQuestions.a: Represent stays as half-open intervals. Store each room's bookings in a `TreeMap` keyed by check-in date. Because bookings of one room never overlap each other, the only booking that can conflict with a new range is the one with the greatest check-in strictly before the new check-out (`lowerEntry(newEnd)`); if its check-out is after the new check-in, there is a conflict. That is O(log n) per room instead of a linear scan.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you prevent two guests from booking the same room for overlapping dates at the same time?
interviewQuestions.a: Make check-and-insert atomic per room. In memory I synchronize on that room's booking map, so concurrent requests for the same room serialize while different rooms proceed in parallel. In a database, model per-night rows (`room_id, date`) with a unique constraint so the second insert fails, or use per-date inventory counts with optimistic locking (`UPDATE ... SET available = available - 1 WHERE available > 0 AND version = ?`).

interviewQuestions.q: Why use half-open date intervals?
interviewQuestions.a: A hotel stay naturally occupies nights from check-in up to, but not including, the check-out date. With `[start, end)`, one guest checking out on the 12th and another checking in on the 12th do not overlap, which is the correct business behaviour. Night counts become `end - start` without off-by-one errors, and the overlap condition `s1 < e2 && s2 < e1` stays simple.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you support different cancellation policies per rate plan?
interviewQuestions.a: Model `CancellationPolicy` as a strategy with `refund(booking, today)`: fully refundable until 7 days before, 50% until 2 days, non-refundable, and so on. Attach the chosen policy to each booking at booking time (its rate plan) so later policy changes do not affect existing reservations. The cancellation flow simply calls `booking.policy().refund(...)`, and new policies are just new classes.

problems.title: Design a Pub-Sub Message Queue
problems.summary: Build a Kafka-inspired in-memory message queue with topics, multiple subscribers, per-subscriber offsets, async consumer workers and replay.
keyPoints: Store messages in an append-only topic log; subscribers keep independent offsets (Kafka model).
Fan-out is free: every subscriber reads the same log at its own pace, and offsets enable replay.
Each subscription has a worker that waits when caught up and is notified on publish (guarded wait in a loop).
Publishing is O(1) and never blocks on slow consumers.
Broker is a Facade over topics, handlers and workers; Observer/Pub-Sub decouples producers and consumers.
Failure handling: retry with backoff, then dead-letter topic; commit the offset after successful processing for at-least-once.
Consumer groups and partitions are the standard scaling extensions.

interviewQuestions.q: Why use offsets instead of deleting messages after delivery?
interviewQuestions.a: With an append-only log and per-subscriber offsets, each subscriber progresses independently: a slow email service does not delay analytics, and neither blocks the publisher. Messages are written once regardless of subscriber count (no per-subscriber copies). Replay becomes trivial - reset the offset - which is invaluable for recovering from bugs or onboarding a new consumer. Retention policies then delete old messages by time or size rather than on consumption. This is exactly Kafka's design.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you guarantee ordering and at-least-once delivery?
interviewQuestions.a: Ordering per subscriber comes from a single worker processing messages sequentially by offset. For at-least-once, the offset is committed only after `consume` succeeds; if the consumer crashes mid-processing, it restarts from the last committed offset and may see a message twice, so consumers must be idempotent (dedupe by message id). At-most-once commits before processing. Exactly-once needs idempotent consumers plus transactional offset commits.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you implement consumer groups?
interviewQuestions.a: A consumer group is a set of subscribers that share the work: each message goes to only one member. Either keep one shared offset per group and let members atomically claim the next offset (`getAndIncrement`), which loses strict ordering, or split the topic into partitions and assign each partition to exactly one member, which preserves per-partition order. Rebalancing reassigns partitions when members join or leave.

interviewQuestions.q: What happens if a subscriber keeps failing on a message?
interviewQuestions.a: It must not block the subscriber forever (a poison message). Retry a bounded number of times with exponential backoff; if it still fails, publish the message plus error details to a dead-letter topic and advance the offset. Operators can inspect the dead-letter topic and replay messages after a fix. My demo simply logs and skips; a `RetryPolicy` strategy would make this configurable per subscriber.

problems.title: Design an Inventory & Order Management System
problems.summary: An e-commerce core (Flipkart/Amazon style): products, warehouse inventory with reservations, cart, order lifecycle with State transitions, payment and Observer notifications.
keyPoints: Reserve stock first, then pay; commit on success, release on failure (two-phase, no overselling).
Reserve all cart items all-or-nothing, locking items in sorted product-id order to avoid deadlocks.
Order status enum with canMoveTo encodes the lifecycle; illegal transitions throw.
Observers handle customer notifications, analytics and low-stock alerts without coupling to core logic.
OrderService is a Facade over catalog, inventory, payment and observers.
Store prices in paise (long) and snapshot unit prices into OrderItems at order time.
At scale: conditional SQL updates or Redis atomic ops for stock, and Sagas with compensations across services.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you prevent overselling when many users order the last unit simultaneously?
interviewQuestions.a: Make the check-and-decrement atomic. In-memory, each inventory item is locked while checking `available >= qty` and moving units to `reserved`; only one thread can take the last unit. Across multiple items, I lock in a sorted order and roll back partial reservations. In a database, a conditional update - `UPDATE inventory SET available = available - 1 WHERE id = ? AND available >= 1` - succeeds for exactly one transaction (check affected rows). Flash sales add Redis counters and queues in front.

interviewQuestions.q: Why reserve inventory before payment instead of deducting directly?
interviewQuestions.a: Payment takes time and can fail. Deducting only after payment risks selling the same unit twice; deducting before payment and failing leaves inventory wrong unless carefully reverted. Reservation moves units from `available` to `reserved`: other buyers cannot take them, and the outcome is explicit - commit on success, release on failure or timeout. Reservations with expiry also protect against abandoned checkouts.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you model the order lifecycle?
interviewQuestions.a: As a state machine. I use an `OrderStatus` enum where each state declares its allowed next states (`CREATED -> PAID | PAYMENT_FAILED | CANCELLED`, `PAID -> SHIPPED | CANCELLED`, `SHIPPED -> DELIVERED`). `Order.transitionTo` validates and records the change, then observers are notified. If states gain rich behaviour (refund rules, SLA timers), I would upgrade to full State pattern classes. Persisting each transition gives an audit trail.

interviewQuestions.q: How would this work across microservices (order, inventory, payment)?
interviewQuestions.a: Distributed transactions with 2PC are avoided; instead use a **Saga**. The order service creates a PENDING order and emits an event; inventory reserves stock and emits StockReserved or StockFailed; payment charges and emits PaymentDone or PaymentFailed. Each failure triggers compensating actions (release stock, cancel order, refund). Use the outbox pattern for reliable event publishing and idempotent consumers to handle duplicate events.

problems.title: Design a Cab Booking System (Uber/Ola LLD)
problems.summary: Design ride booking with riders, drivers, location-based driver matching, ride lifecycle, fare strategies and concurrency-safe driver assignment.
keyPoints: Driver availability is assigned atomically with compareAndSet(AVAILABLE, ON_TRIP); losers try the next candidate.
Matching returns an ordered candidate list from a pluggable DriverMatchingStrategy (nearest, rating, ETA).
Fare is a Strategy; surge pricing is a Decorator wrapping any base fare.
Ride lifecycle transitions are guarded: ACCEPTED -> STARTED -> COMPLETED, or CANCELLED before start.
Haversine distance is fine for demos; production uses geohash, quadtrees or H3 plus road ETA.
Releasing the driver and updating their location happen on completion or cancellation.
Extensions: accept/reject with timeouts, pooling, per-zone surge, location streaming.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you ensure a driver is not assigned to two riders at once?
interviewQuestions.a: Driver status is an `AtomicReference<DriverStatus>`; assignment calls `compareAndSet(AVAILABLE, ON_TRIP)`, which succeeds for exactly one thread. Matching returns a ranked list of candidates, and each request walks the list until a CAS succeeds or the list is exhausted. There is no global lock, so unrelated requests proceed in parallel. In a distributed system the same idea becomes a conditional update in the database or a Redis `SET driver:lock NX` with TTL.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you find nearby drivers efficiently for millions of drivers?
interviewQuestions.a: Use a spatial index instead of scanning. Geohash encodes lat/long into a string where shared prefixes mean proximity; store drivers in buckets by geohash cell and query the rider's cell plus its 8 neighbours. Alternatives: quadtrees (adaptive cell sizes for dense cities) or Uber's H3 hexagonal grid. Drivers send location pings every few seconds, updating their cell. Candidates are then ranked by road ETA from a routing service rather than straight-line distance.

interviewQuestions.q: Why model surge pricing as a Decorator?
interviewQuestions.a: Surge multiplies whatever the base fare is, independent of how the base is calculated (per km, per minute, flat airport fare). As a decorator implementing `FareStrategy`, `SurgeFare` wraps any base strategy and can be combined with others, such as a `PromoDiscount` decorator, in any order. The ride service still calls `fareStrategy.fare(ride)` and does not know whether surge applies. Adding or removing surge is a configuration change.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you implement drivers accepting or rejecting ride offers?
interviewQuestions.a: After matching, the ride enters a `SEARCHING` state and the system offers it to the best candidate, tentatively reserving them with the CAS. A scheduled task times out the offer after N seconds. On accept, the ride moves to `ACCEPTED`; on reject or timeout, the driver is released and the next candidate is offered the ride. After exhausting candidates or a global timeout, the ride is cancelled with "no drivers". Offer events are pushed to driver apps via WebSockets or push notifications.

problems.title: Design an In-Memory Key-Value Store
problems.summary: A Redis-like in-memory store with typed attribute values, TTL expiry, secondary-index search, transactions and thread safety - a popular machine-coding problem.
keyPoints: Fix each attribute's type on first use with ConcurrentHashMap.putIfAbsent and reject later mismatches.
A secondary index attr -> value -> keys makes search fast but must be updated on every put and delete.
Data and index change together, so guard both with one ReentrantReadWriteLock (many readers, one writer).
TTL uses lazy expiry on reads plus an active background sweeper, like Redis.
Transactions buffer writes (with tombstones for deletes) and apply them atomically under the write lock.
Inject a clock so TTL behaviour is testable without sleeping.
Scale via sharding by key hash; persistence via append-only logs and snapshots.

interviewQuestions.q: How does your design support fast search by attribute value?
interviewQuestions.a: I maintain a secondary (inverted) index: `Map<attribute, Map<value, Set<key>>>`. On `put`, I first remove the key's old attributes from the index, then add the new ones; on `delete`, I remove them. `search(attr, value)` is then two hash lookups plus copying the matching keys, instead of scanning every entry. The trade-off is extra memory and write cost, which is acceptable for read-heavy workloads. Index and data are updated under the same write lock to stay consistent.

interviewQuestions.q: Why a ReadWriteLock instead of ConcurrentHashMap?
interviewQuestions.a: A `ConcurrentHashMap` makes single-map operations thread-safe, but a put here touches several structures - the data map and multiple index buckets - which must change atomically together, otherwise a concurrent search could see a key in the index whose data is gone. A `ReentrantReadWriteLock` lets many readers (`get`, `search`) run in parallel while writers get exclusive access. For heavy write throughput, I would shard the store so each shard has its own lock.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you implement key expiry (TTL)?
interviewQuestions.a: Each entry stores an absolute `expiresAt`. **Lazy expiry**: every read checks it and treats expired keys as absent. **Active expiry**: a `ScheduledExecutorService` periodically removes expired keys so keys that are never read again do not leak memory. Redis does both, and its active cycle samples random keys to bound CPU. Alternatively, keep a min-heap or `TreeMap` of expiry times to remove only the keys that are due.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you implement transactions with rollback?
interviewQuestions.a: A transaction keeps a private write buffer: puts store the new attributes, deletes store a tombstone. Reads inside the transaction check the buffer first (read-your-own-writes) and fall back to the store. `commit` acquires the store's write lock and applies all buffered operations at once, so other clients see all or none of them; `rollback` simply discards the buffer. For isolation against concurrent writers, record key versions at read time and abort the commit if any changed (optimistic concurrency control).
